title: Risotto alla Milanese
subtitle: Saffron risotto from Milan
excerpt: The gold standard of Italian risotto: Arborio or Carnaroli rice stirred with bone marrow, white wine, and a concentrated saffron infusion until the grains are swollen and the risotto flows like lava. Finished with cold butter and parmesan.

recipe.sourceNotes: Risotto alla milanese is the defining dish of Milan and the most celebrated risotto in the world. It is traditionally the accompaniment to osso buco, the two dishes together forming one of the great pairings in Italian cooking. The colour comes from saffron: the authentic version uses a concentrated infusion of saffron steeped in warm broth or white wine. Bone marrow (the marrow from split beef bones) is traditional and gives the risotto a distinctive richness; butter is the modern substitute. The technique is the same as all risotti: warm stock is added ladle by ladle, with constant stirring, and the process must never be rushed. The final step, mantecatura, involves removing the pan from the heat and beating in cold butter and grated parmesan until the risotto becomes glossy and emulsified.

content.text: Keep the stock hot throughout; cold stock cools the rice and slows the cooking, producing a gluey result. The final mantecatura (beating in cold butter off the heat) is not optional: it is what makes risotto creamy and glossy rather than starchy and heavy. The finished risotto should flow slowly if the pot is tilted; all'onda, the Venetian term, means it should move like a wave.

content.text: Melt 40 g butter in a wide, heavy pan over medium-low heat. Cook the onion for 8 minutes, stirring, until completely soft but not coloured. Add the rice and stir for 2 minutes until each grain is coated in butter and slightly translucent at the edges. Add the wine and stir until absorbed.

Add the saffron broth (strain the saffron strands if you prefer, or leave them in). Add the stock one ladle at a time, stirring constantly and waiting until each addition is absorbed before adding the next. This takes 18 to 20 minutes total. The rice is done when the grain is tender to the bite with just a tiny firm centre.

Remove from the heat. Season with salt and pepper. Add the cold butter cut into small pieces and the grated parmesan. Beat vigorously with a wooden spoon for 1 to 2 minutes until the butter is fully incorporated and the risotto is glossy and creamy. Cover and rest for 2 minutes. Serve immediately in warm bowls.
